::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This is not my paper, and these are not my ideas.** Everything in this post comes from *LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models* by Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun (arXiv:2610.15267, October 2026). The method, the proofs, the experiments, the numbers and the conclusions are theirs. I am only trying to explain, in plain words, what the paper says and what it means.

**How to read the citations.** Every statement about the method or the results is followed by where it comes from in the paper, for example (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2, Table 7). If a sentence has no citation, it is my rewording of the cited sentences around it, not a new claim. Any mistake in the explanation is mine, not the authors'. When in doubt, the paper is the source of truth.

**About the figures.** Figures 1 to 4 are small illustrations I drew to make the paper's ideas visible, using a textbook pendulum. They are not results of the paper and not its trained models. Figure 5 redraws numbers reported in the paper's Tables 7 and 2. The code for all five is in [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**In short.** According to the authors, a world model that predicts by feeding its own output back in can slowly shrink its latent space over a long rollout (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). Their method, LeHami, replaces the usual predictor with a learned Hamiltonian flow stepped by a leapfrog integrator, which they prove keeps phase-space volume exactly at every step (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2, Proposition 1). On two pendulum environments they report much better velocity prediction than an unconstrained JEPA baseline, with fewer parameters and less training compute (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2; Appendix E.1, Tables 4, 5 and 7). They also report that a baseline with an untied three-frame window still plans better on some goals (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4, Table 2). In their own words, volume preservation "forbids the degenerate failures but it does not bound the growth of rollout error" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2).

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## The paper in five points

- **The problem is predictor contraction.** In an autoregressive rollout, a small per-step contraction compounds over the horizon (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). The authors show that the optimum of a one-step squared loss is a conditional mean, which contracts (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 3).
- **The fix is geometric.** A leapfrog step on a learned separable Hamiltonian is exactly symplectic for every step size, parameter and action, so it rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points and the merging of distinct states (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1, Proposition 2).
- **Momentum is not learned.** A fixed Savitzky–Golay stencil reads it off the encoder trajectory (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1; Appendix C.4). Because the stencil is odd in time, the sign of velocity is kept (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3).
- **The reported gain is mostly in velocity.** 2.80× lower velocity error over rollout steps 1–10 and 1.52× over steps 21–70 on the conservative pendulum (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Table 7), and a constant latent volume where the baseline contracts steadily (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2, Fig. 4 right).
- **It is not a win on every task.** The baseline reaches goal angles more often, and its untied three-frame variant has the highest success on velocity goals (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4, Table 2; §4).
:::

## 1. The problem the paper starts from

A JEPA world model learns to predict in latent space rather than in pixels (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). To look far ahead, it is rolled out: "each prediction is fed back as the next input" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1).

The authors note that existing JEPA work successfully prevents *encoder collapse*, mapping distinct inputs to the same representation, with training-time regularization or frozen backbones (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). They point to a second problem, *predictor contraction*: "even a slight per-step contraction of the transition map compounds over the horizon and progressively shrinks the latent distribution" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1).

They also explain why this should be expected. Under any observation or latent noise, the minimiser of a one-step squared error is the conditional mean of the next state, "which averages away whatever the anchor leaves undetermined: it contracts volume, and it sends latents that differ only in the averaged-out directions to a common image" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 3). In plain words: the training loss itself pulls an unconstrained predictor toward this failure.

They measure it. On the conservative pendulum, the cumulative log-determinant of LeHami's one-step map stays at exactly 0, while the baseline, LeWorldModel (LeWM), "exhibits a steady linear decline in cumulative log-volume" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2, Fig. 4 right). The same holds for the full phase-space volume of the baseline's three-embedding context (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.2, Fig. 13).

## 2. The idea: use the structure of classical mechanics

The authors' starting point is that "physics avoids this contraction through geometric structure" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). Hamiltonian mechanics describes a system by a single scalar $H$ and preserves phase-space volume (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1). In their background section they put it this way: a cloud of initial conditions "may stretch, rotate and shear, but its volume is invariant" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix B). They add that volume preservation persists under actuation, provided the action enters the Hamiltonian (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1).

LeHami brings this into the latent space. The encoder outputs a position-like block $q_t$, the momentum-like block $p_t$ is derived from it, and the pair is advanced by Hamilton's equations for a learned scalar $H_\phi$ (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, Eqs. 1–2):

$$
\dot q = \frac{\partial H_\phi}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p = -\frac{\partial H_\phi}{\partial q}, \qquad H_\phi(q, p, u) = K_{\phi_1}(p) + V_{\phi_2}(q, u).
$$

Two design choices stand out in the paper. First, the action $u$ is placed in the potential, so the generalized force it produces is a gradient in $q$ for every action, and the step stays exactly symplectic as long as $u$ is constant within a step (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, "Action-conditioned Hamiltonian"; Appendix C.4, Eq. 9). Second, the Hamiltonian is *separable*, kinetic energy in $p$ and potential in $q$ and $u$, which "enables fast, explicit leapfrog integration without requiring iterative numerical solvers" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, "Design choices").

The authors are explicit about what LeHami is *not*. "We are not modeling the physics of the observed system": $H_\phi$ is never fitted to a known Hamiltonian, and the true equations of motion enter only as targets for frozen evaluation probes (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 5). They describe this as the point of departure from Hamiltonian neural networks and symplectic recurrent networks, where recovering the physical Hamiltonian is the goal (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 5). In LeHami, $q_t$ is not even assumed to encode position, nor $p_t$ momentum, in any observation-space sense (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 5).

## 3. The leapfrog step and what it guarantees

The integrator is the leapfrog (Störmer–Verlet) step, which the authors choose because it is "second-order accurate and, crucially, exactly symplectic" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1). It is a half kick on the momentum, a full drift on the position, and another half kick (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, Eq. 4). A learned diagonal scale $S = \mathrm{diag}(e^\sigma)$ absorbs the relative scale of $q$ and $p$, which the self-supervised objective leaves undetermined; since $S$ is a constant linear rescaling, the flow stays exactly symplectic (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, Eq. 3; Appendix C.4).

The proof is in the appendix (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1, Proposition 2). Here is my summary of its steps. The authors write the step as three maps, each changing only one block (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Eq. 7). The Jacobian of each is block-triangular with identities on the diagonal, so its determinant is 1 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1). The off-diagonal block is a Hessian, which is symmetric, and that symmetry makes each map symplectic (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1). Compositions of symplectic diffeomorphisms remain symplectic diffeomorphisms, so the full step and all its iterates are too, for every step size $h > 0$, every control $u$ and every parameter $\phi$ (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1).

![**Figure 2.** An illustration of the structure of the leapfrog step in the paper's Eq. 4 and its proof in Appendix C.1. A square cell of states is pushed by a half kick (only $p$ changes, by an amount set by $q$), then a drift (only $q$ changes, by an amount set by $p$), then another half kick. Each shear bends the cell; none changes its area. Drawn by me with a pendulum-like potential; not a figure or result of the paper.](figures/fig02.png){fig-alt="Four panels on a light grid. A grey square, then the same area pushed vertically into a slanted shape, then pushed horizontally into a tilted shape, then pushed vertically again. Under each panel: area equals 1.0000."}

From this, the authors derive three failure modes that cannot occur (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1, Proposition 2 (i)–(iii)):

1. **No uniform contraction.** The singular values of the $K$-step Jacobian multiply to 1, so the largest is at least 1 and the smallest at most 1 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Proposition 2 (i)).
2. **No asymptotically stable fixed point.** The proof shows that an attracting fixed point would squeeze a ball of positive volume into an arbitrarily small one, contradicting volume preservation (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.1, proof of (ii)).
3. **No merging.** Every iterate is a diffeomorphism, hence injective, so "two latents that differ at the anchor remain distinct at every horizon" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Proposition 2 (iii)).

The authors also state what the guarantee does not give. It is about "shape, not size": a cloud that cannot be squeezed can still be stretched, so symplecticity "places no bound on the growth of rollout error and does not make the rollout accurate" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 3). It does not make regularization redundant: the SIGReg regularizer shapes the encoder distribution during training, while symplecticity carries the volume of whatever distribution it is handed at inference, and the authors describe the two as "complementary rather than substitutes" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.2, Remark 4).

They explain why they chose the Hamiltonian over the Lagrangian formulation: the volume guarantee is a property of a flow on phase space, and a separable $H$ keeps the leapfrog explicit and exactly symplectic at any step size (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.3).

## 4. Momentum read off, not learned

In LeHami, the momentum-like block is never learned (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.2). It is obtained with a Savitzky–Golay stencil: a least-squares quadratic fit to the encoded positions in a short window, differentiated at the current frame (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1, "Design choices"; Appendix C.4). The authors stress that the stencil "adds no learned parameters and cannot itself collapse" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §2.1), and that whatever the momentum block carries, "it carries because the encoder trajectory moves" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4).

Two stencils are used. A causal one, over the current and three previous positions, initialises each rollout, so the model never reads frames it is about to predict (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4; Appendix D.2). A centred five-frame one, with weights $(-2,-1,0,1,2)/10$, builds the momentum targets for the loss (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4). The authors report that the centred stencil amplifies per-frame encoder noise 24.5× less than the causal one, and that its antisymmetry maps $p_t \mapsto -p_t$ exactly under time reversal (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4).

The stencil also explains why no mass is learned. Defining $p$ as $\dot q$ already fixes the mass matrix to the identity in the learned coordinates, and for a constant-mass system the encoder can absorb the true mass through a linear re-coordinatization (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4, Eqs. 11–12). The authors note the limit: when the mass matrix depends on configuration, as in a double pendulum, $p = \dot q$ is a velocity rather than a canonical momentum, and lifting this requires learning $p$ jointly (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4).

### Why the sign of velocity matters

A natural alternative is to give the encoder several frames. The paper explains why this can fail (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.1; Appendix E.3, Eq. 16). With a three-frame temporal kernel whose outer weights are tied, $(a, b, a)$, reversing the frame order leaves the output unchanged, so the states $(\theta, +\omega)$ and $(\theta, -\omega)$ map to the same latent (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.1). The paper's numbers: the tied three-frame baseline decodes speed $|\omega|$ at $R^2 = 0.921$, but signed velocity $\omega$ at $R^2 = -0.115$ (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Table 9).

The Savitzky–Golay stencil is an odd operator: "reversing time sends $m \to -m$ and hence the estimate to $-1$ times itself" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3). The authors summarise: the Hamiltonian model gets velocity "not by seeing more frames or learning unrestricted asymmetric weights, but by applying an antisymmetric structural operator to them" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3).

The tied window $(a, b, a)$ gives the same value for $+\omega$ and $-\omega$ (the paper's Eq. 16, computed here with $a = b$). The centred Savitzky–Golay stencil, with the weights given in the paper's Appendix C.4, gives a value whose sign follows $\omega$. Drawn by me; not a result of the paper.](figures/fig03.png){fig-alt="Left: two lines of five dots crossing at the middle frame, one rising, one falling. Right: a red curve nearly flat near 1 and symmetric about zero velocity; a blue straight line through the origin from minus 1 to plus 1."}

This matters for planning: the authors report that 92% of the planning goals require the correct sign of velocity, so an agent arriving at the goal spinning the wrong way fails the velocity criterion whatever its speed (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3; Fig. 16).

## 5. One flow, any step size, both directions

Because $H_\phi$ parameterizes a continuous vector field, the authors note that one trained model can be integrated at different step sizes without retraining (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1, item ii; §3.3). Trained only at $\Delta t = 0.1$ s, the model traces the same trajectory when integrated at $\Delta t/2$ and $\Delta t/4$, compared against a Runge–Kutta integration of the true equation; doubling the step breaks it, "as an explicit symplectic integrator leaves its stability band" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.3, Fig. 5 left).

Time reversal works the same way: flipping $\Delta t \to -\Delta t$ in $H_\phi$ and rolling back gives a round-trip error that stays below $10^{-4}\%$ (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.3, Fig. 5 right). The authors call the reversal approximate rather than exact, in part because the rollout's anchor uses the causal stencil, which is not odd under reversal (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.2).

![**Figure 4.** An illustration of the two properties in the paper's §3.3, on a textbook pendulum with its exact energy. Left: angle error against an exact solution for three step sizes. Right: run $K$ steps forward, flip the sign of $h$, run $K$ steps back; with the exact energy only floating-point rounding is left. Drawn by me; these are not the paper's results. The paper's learned model is in its Fig. 5: it reports a round-trip error below $10^{-4}\%$ and a breakdown at $2\Delta t$, which my exact pendulum does not show.](figures/fig04.png){fig-alt="Left: three error curves on a log scale over four seconds; the coarsest step is highest near 10 to the minus 2, the finest lowest near 10 to the minus 5. Right: round-trip error on a log scale stays between 10 to the minus 17 and 10 to the minus 15 for up to 60 steps."}

The authors present time reversal as a primitive for computing backward reachable tubes and online safety guarantees in optimal control (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §1, item iii). The paper does not run such experiments. It also describes, but does not test, training across recording rates: every model in the paper is trained and evaluated at a single rate (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.2).

## 6. The experiments

The paper evaluates two pendulum environments rendered as 64×64 RGB images: a conservative pendulum with three rod lengths, and an actuated pendulum driven by a recorded torque, with three rod lengths and three masses (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3, Fig. 3; Appendix D.3, Table 3).

LeHami is designed as a drop-in replacement for the predictor of a JEPA world model, so the authors compare it with LeWorldModel, replacing only the predictor and adding the fixed stencil (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.1). Encoder, projector, optimiser, data pipeline, schedule and multi-step objective are shared, "so a difference in rollout behavior is not attributable to the training scheme" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.1). Physical state is read by three probes of increasing capacity, ridge, $k$-NN ($k = 25$) and a two-layer MLP, each fitted once and frozen (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.1, "Probing").

**Velocity in rollout.** On the conservative pendulum, the two models are level on angle early, and LeHami pulls ahead from about step 11 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2, Fig. 4 left). On velocity, the paper reports 0.364 against 1.020 rad/s over steps 1–10 and 1.534 against 2.331 over steps 21–70 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Table 7). At the anchor, velocity decoded from the frozen encoder features reaches $R^2 = +0.975$ for LeHami and $-0.667$ for LeWM (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Table 7). The authors explain that one image does not show motion, so a per-frame encoder cannot supply velocity, while LeHami reads it from the stencil (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2). They also show that LeHami's rollouts stay on their own level set of $H_\phi$, while LeWM's cross them (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2; Appendix E.2, Figs. 10–11).

**Compute and parameters.** The paper reports about 32% fewer parameters for LeHami, 3.03 M against 4.44 M, the difference sitting in the predictor: 2.23 M for the two Hamiltonian MLPs against 3.31 M for LeWM's transformer (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.1, Table 5). At every matched training budget, LeHami's error is 1.45–4.2× lower on angle and 1.4–2.3× lower on velocity, and its 0.75 PFLOP checkpoint already beats LeWM's best within 6 PFLOP (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.1, Table 4). These budget results are from one seed per model (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.1, Table 4).

**Encoder independence.** With a tiny ViT, LeHami decodes velocity at the anchor at $R^2 = 0.929$, and with a ConvNet at 0.939, while the baseline scores $-0.031$ and $-0.018$ (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.2). With a frozen pre-trained DINOv2 encoder, DINO-LeHami outperforms DINO-WM (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2; Appendix E.2, Fig. 12), with a smaller advantage on angle than on velocity (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.2).

**With actions.** On the actuated pendulum at the anchor, LeHami's MLP probe reads velocity at $R^2 = 0.987$, while all three of LeWM's probe tiers stay below the predict-the-mean floor; on angle, LeWM decodes $\theta$ more accurately (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2, Table 1). The authors attribute the angle gap to LeHami splitting its capacity into $q$ and $p$ of 32 dimensions each, half of LeWM's 64 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3). Along the rollout, LeHami keeps better velocity prediction until about step 10, when the baseline's predictor "has ingested enough context frames to implicitly infer motion" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.2; Fig. 15).

## 7. Planning results

Planning is evaluated on the actuated pendulum (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.4.2). Goals are recorded states of held-out episodes 30 frames after the start, the action sequence is optimised in each model's latent space with the Cross-Entropy Method under model-predictive control, and the budget is at most 15 TFLOP per episode (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.1, "Planning"; §3.4; Appendix D.4.2). An episode succeeds when the angle is within 0.1 rad and the velocity within 0.5 rad/s of the goal (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix D.4.2).

The paper's Table 2 reports (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4, Table 2):

- **Position goals:** single-frame LeWM 0.800, LeHami 0.480.
- **Velocity goals:** single-frame LeWM 0.184, LeHami 0.527, untied three-frame LeWM 0.800.
- **Position and velocity:** untied three-frame LeWM 0.636, tied three-frame LeWM 0.400, LeHami 0.304.

The authors explain the single-frame baseline's failure on velocity: its per-frame goal embedding carries no velocity (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4). A tied window captures speed but not direction, and only an untied window captures signed velocity, at a high cost per solve that forces longer replanning intervals under the budget (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4).

They then split the velocity criterion into speed and sign (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3, Table 10). On the sign, LeHami reaches 0.800, against 0.656 and 0.649 for single-frame and tied LeWM, which sit slightly below the 0.680 floor of applying no torque; only untied LeWM does better, at 0.962 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3, Table 10). The authors note LeHami does this "without a learned temporal kernel and at 0.59× the compute" (8.05 against 13.65 TFLOP) (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3). Among plans that reach the goal angle, LeHami's final velocity has the goal's sign in 91–95% of cases (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3). What limits its joint success is reaching the goal angle: 48% of plans at a replanning interval of 9, against 63% and 70% for tied and untied three-frame LeWM; the authors conclude that "the bottleneck is positional goal-reaching, not the direction of the velocity" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3).

On compute, over 99% of a planning episode's arithmetic is the predictor rollout, where LeHami's MLP flow costs 13.6 MFLOP per step per candidate against 21.7 for LeWM, so an episode costs LeHami 0.63× the baseline's FLOPs (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.3, "Planning compute"). This lets LeHami replan more often within the same budget (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4). The authors' own reading: untied LeWM achieves a higher success rate, LeHami "provides a structurally rigorous alternative", and replacing the fixed stencil with a jointly learned momentum "offers a clear path to closing this performance gap" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3.4).

## 8. The limits the authors state

The paper lists its own limitations (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4, "Limitations and future work"):

- **Dissipation.** Strongly dissipative systems, such as those with heavy friction, contract phase-space volume, so extending LeHami to them, for example with port-Hamiltonian extensions, is left to future work (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4; Appendix C.4). The appendix sketches how: a learned positive semi-definite damping matrix in the momentum equation (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4).
- **Task type.** LeHami targets velocity-aware tasks; purely static pose tasks "are served well by spatial-focused, unconstrained predictors" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4).
- **The fixed stencil.** Replacing it with a learned momentum-like embedding could improve performance without giving up long-horizon phase-space stability (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4).

Other caveats appear in the appendices. The latent-space $R^2$ checks are measured in the model's own coordinates and, "being self-referential", cannot alone establish that a physical quantity survives; in them the momentum block drops below zero by step 25 while the position block is at 0.646 (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix E.2, Table 6). Several analyses use one training seed per model (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Table 4, Figs. 4 right, 12 and 13). The configuration-dependent mass case, such as a double pendulum, is noted as one where the stencil's argument no longer holds (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Appendix C.4). Both environments in the paper are single pendulums (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §3; Appendix D.3).

## 9. The paper's conclusion, in short

The authors conclude that LeHami's exact symplectic step gives structural guarantees: exact volume preservation, which provably eliminates some rollout collapse modes, and continuous-time integration with time reversal (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4). Empirically, on the conservative pendulum LeHami preserves latent volume where LeWM contracts steadily, and predicts velocity better throughout and angle better at long horizons (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4). With actuation, LeWM reaches the goal angle more often but captures signed velocity only when its temporal window is explicitly untied, while LeHami captures angle and signed velocity by construction (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4). In their framing, this paves "the way towards velocity-constrained planning and FLOP-efficient replanning" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, §4), and more broadly shows "how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models" (Yalovetzky et al., 2026, Abstract).

## Reference

Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun, ["LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15267), arXiv:2610.15267 [cs.LG] (2026). Code: [github.com/rominay/LeHami](https://github.com/rominay/LeHami).
